The correct adjustment is to barrel less often but more polarized: your best value hands, the ones that welcome a big pot, keep firing, and your weakest bluff candidates are best turned into semi-bluffs that have real river plans, like backdoor flush draws that would love to hit a heart.
Meanwhile, your medium-strength hands, second pair with a decent kicker for example, should mostly check for pot control.
As always, the key discipline is asking whether each hand you are considering barreling has a plausible river plan, and if not, whether checking gets you a better result on the turn.

sections.title: Scenario: Barreling the Two of Diamonds
lines: Chapter eight, section four. Scenario, barreling the two of diamonds.
Now imagine the turn is the two of diamonds, a low card that misses her range almost entirely.
It also completes some backdoor flush draws in your favor, since your range has more high-diamond combinations than hers.
Two of diamonds is a bad card for her and a small equity bump for you, so the correct adjustment is to barrel more often and slightly bigger.
Your best value hands can size up, because the caller's range is capped and cannot punish you for polarizing.
Your weakest bluffs, hands you gave up on the flop, can even come out of the check-back range and turn into speculative turn bluffs, since her folding frequency should be high.
This is a scenario where leverage really shines: a well-executed turn barrel here sets up a threatening river shove that many caller ranges simply cannot handle.
The rule of thumb is: when the turn card misses the caller's range and modestly helps yours, the correct move is more barreling, at a size that lets the river run naturally.

sections.title: Test Yourself
lines: Chapter eight, section five. Test yourself.
Question one. Flop is queen-jack-two rainbow, you c-bet small, the big blind calls. Turn is the ace of spades. Good, bad, or neutral for you?
Good. The ace fits your range far better than hers. Barrel more often, and size up with your strongest value.
Question two. Same start, but the turn is the ten of hearts. Good, bad, or neutral?
Bad. The ten completes many straight draws and gives new equity to hands like nine-eight and king-nine. Slow down, keep firing only with your strongest value and best semi-bluffs.
Question three. You barrel the turn with king-queen offsuit on a board where the river will let you value bet many hearts. What size do you want?
One that grows the pot geometrically toward a comfortable river bet. Aim for around two-thirds of the pot in most cases; too small strands leverage, too big over-commits.
Question four. Your c-bet was called on a very dynamic board and the turn is a card that helps neither range much. What is the correct plan?
Check most hands. On a neutral card after a wet flop, both ranges are still murky, and checking preserves optionality without conceding the pot.
The habit is: read the turn card first, choose the size second, and pick the exact hands last.

sections.title: Conclusion
lines: Chapter eight, section six. Conclusion.
Barreling the turn is a range-construction problem, not a hand-strength problem.
Your first question should always be about how the turn card changed the balance of ranges, not about how it changed your specific hand.
The good-turn, bad-turn, neutral-turn triage lets you set frequency and size in seconds, freeing your attention for the harder hand-by-hand choices.
Every semi-bluff should have a river plan; if it does not, checking is almost always better than betting.
Turn barrels are only as good as the river bets they set up, so plan the river before you fire the turn.
In the next chapter we look at what happens when the aggressor gives up and checks the flop, and how to exploit that missed continuation bet from the caller's seat.

chapters.title: Chapter 9: Attacking a Missed Continuation Bet

sections.title: Overview & Objectives
lines: Chapter nine, section one. Overview and objectives.
Most of the chapters so far have looked at the world from the aggressor's seat.
This chapter changes seats: when the pre-flop raiser checks the flop, the caller has a big opportunity, and this chapter is about how to take it.
A missed continuation bet is a message: the aggressor probably does not have a strong hand, or he would have bet.
The caller can use that message to attack the turn with a wider, more polarized range, because the aggressor's checking range is capped.
By the end of this chapter you should be able to build a probing range on the turn after the aggressor checks the flop.
You should be able to combine value hands and bluffs in the right proportions, exploiting the aggressor's capped range without over-bluffing into his slowplays.
You should be able to plan turn probes on different board textures, adjusting for how easily the aggressor's range can defend.
And you should recognize the specific spots where a big turn bet after a missed c-bet becomes almost a free money maker.

sections.title: Scenario: Evaluating the Turn After a Check
lines: Chapter nine, section two. Scenario, evaluating the turn after a check.
Picture the button opens, the big blind calls, and the flop is king of clubs, seven of hearts, four of spades.
The button checks behind, a slightly unusual line but one that shows up when the button decides the range dynamics are not favorable enough to c-bet.
The turn arrives, and the big blind gets to lead.
The first question is what the button's checked flop range looks like: mostly low pairs, ace-high with backdoor equity, and a small slowplay contingent.

The big blind's leading range should be wider than her normal betting range against a c-bet, because the aggressor's checked range is capped and unable to fight back with a real polarized range of its own.

The rule of thumb is: on turns that further tighten the caller's expected value from checking, the big blind should probe often and small, extracting the aggressor's give-up range while charging his medium hands.
On turns that shift equity back toward the aggressor, the big blind should probe less and consider checking to induce a delayed c-bet.

sections.title: Scenario: Attacking the Seven of Hearts
lines: Chapter nine, section three. Scenario, attacking the seven of hearts.
Suppose the turn is a card that clearly favors the big blind, like the seven of hearts on a king-high flop.
Now she has a bunch of new two-pair combinations, more straight draws, and no reason to fear that the aggressor has caught up.
She should lead most of her value hands, mix in a wide range of semi-bluffs like flush draws and combo draws, and even include some pure bluffs with backdoor equity.
The aggressor, holding a capped range, cannot raise credibly, and the big blind's turn bet is extracting maximum value from his medium hands while denying equity to his weak overcards.

The right size is often a small-to-medium bet, one-third to one-half of the pot, because a big polarized bet risks folding out too many of the aggressor's calling hands and does not extract the full value from the weak-called range.

This is a spot where the range advantage compounds: the aggressor already showed weakness, and the turn card magnifies that weakness into a directly exploitable frequency mistake if he does not adjust.

sections.title: Scenario: Attacking the Two of Diamonds
lines: Chapter nine, section four. Scenario, attacking the two of diamonds.
Now consider a neutral turn like the two of diamonds after the checked flop.
The two does not change the balance much, so the big blind still has a range edge, but not as sharp as on the seven of hearts.
Her probing range should include her top value hands, some semi-bluffs, and a healthy dose of hands that are only barely worth betting, because the aggressor's give-up frequency is still high.
Size should be small, because the aggressor will fold his weakest hands to almost anything, and calling with the medium hands is still profitable at a small price.
On truly bad turns for the big blind, like an ace that fits the aggressor's range but does not fit hers, she should probe less and consider checking to induce a bluff on the river.
The core skill is calibrating the probing frequency to how much the turn card has tilted the range dynamics.

sections.title: Exploiting a Capped Checking Range
lines: Chapter nine, section five. Exploiting a capped checking range.
The capped checking range is the caller's dream setup, and it applies to more than just missed c-bets.
Any time the aggressor checks a street he would normally bet, his range is capped: no monsters, mostly medium hands and give-ups.
You can exploit a capped checking range in three ways.
First, bet a wider polarized range on the next street, extracting value from the medium hands while giving up on hands you cannot value bet or bluff.
Second, overbet with your strongest value hands, because your opponent's range cannot punish you and folding out his medium hands is often break-even at worst.
Third, use board texture to your advantage: on runouts that make the caller's medium hands even worse, size up further and keep the pressure on.
The one caveat is that some players slowplay strong hands more than the solver would, so if you have a read that a specific opponent slowplays, dial back the bluffing frequency accordingly.
Absent such reads, treat a check as an implicit admission of weakness and press it accordingly.
Some of the highest-EV turn spots in modern poker come precisely from attacking these capped checking ranges.

sections.title: Test Yourself
lines: Chapter nine, section six. Test yourself.
Question one. Button opens, you defend the big blind, flop is king-seven-four rainbow, button checks. Should you bet the turn most of the time?
Yes. The button's checked range is capped; probing the turn extracts value from his medium hands and denies equity to his overcards.
Question two. Same start, turn is the ace of spades. Should you probe?
Less often. The ace helps the button's checked range more than it helps yours; consider checking to induce a delayed c-bet or a bluff on the river.
Question three. You are the button, and after checking the flop, the big blind fires the turn. How should you defend?
Tighter than usual on the calling side, but include some pot-controlling calls with your medium hands. Do not float too widely, because the big blind's range is polarized against your capped range.
Question four. You probed a turn and the big blind called. What is your river plan with a hand that has become a bluff-catcher?
Check-call small bets, fold big bets. Your range on the river is already condensed by the probing action, so you cannot afford to spew off value hands by turning them into desperate bluffs.
The skill is knowing that a check does not just miss value; it hands the caller a lever to move the pot toward her.

sections.title: Conclusion
lines: Chapter nine, section seven. Conclusion.
A missed continuation bet is a gift to the caller, and this chapter has been about learning to unwrap it.
The aggressor's checking range is capped, and capped ranges are attackable in every direction: wider probing, larger sizing, and polarized turn barrels are all on the menu.
The right choice depends on the turn card, but the general framework is that the more the turn favors the caller's original range, the more aggressively she should probe.
Neutral turns still support small, wide probes, because the aggressor's give-up frequency is inherently high.
Bad turns for the caller should slow her down, and often the correct move is to check and induce, converting the aggressor's capped range into a bluff.
In the next chapter we take the aggressor's seat again in the out-of-position role, and we study how to c-bet when you are the one giving away positional advantage on every street.

chapters.title: Chapter 10: C-Betting From Out of Position

sections.title: Overview & Objectives
lines: Chapter ten, section one. Overview and objectives.
So far we have mostly assumed the c-bettor is the in-position player, which is the friendlier side of the game.
This chapter is about the harder version: c-betting when you are out of position, meaning you act first on every post-flop street.
Being out of position costs you information: you have to bet or check before you see what your opponent will do.
You cannot use position to protect your medium hands, and you cannot bluff-catch as cheaply, because your opponent controls the size of the pot.
The good news is that when your range is strong enough, being out of position does not stop you from c-betting effectively.
By the end of this chapter you should be able to identify the range dynamics that support out-of-position c-betting.
You should be able to choose sizes that account for the fact that you cannot see the caller's reaction before you commit.
You should be able to design turn plans that survive being checked to or being raised.
And you should understand when the correct out-of-position plan is to skip the c-bet entirely and defend a checked range instead.

sections.title: Scenario: Out of Position on a Dynamic Board
lines: Chapter ten, section two. Scenario, out of position on a dynamic board.
Picture a small blind versus big blind confrontation where the small blind three-bet pre-flop.
Flop is queen-jack-ten with two hearts, a highly dynamic board where hand values will keep changing.
The small blind is out of position with a range that is strong but not overwhelmingly ahead.
The big blind's calling range is packed with connected and suited hands that hit this board hard.
In this spot, the small blind's best plan is not to c-bet at high frequency; it is to bet a polarized range with clear value and clear semi-bluff candidates, and check the middle of her range.
Sizing matters: a bigger bet suits the polarized dynamic, and it also compensates for the fact that being out of position makes small stabs vulnerable to floats.

The big blind, meanwhile, should defend a wide calling range against the small stabs but be ready to raise polarized against the big bets, because the small blind's out-of-position range is not big enough to defend against a well-timed raise on a dynamic board.

The general theme is that out-of-position c-betting rewards a polarized shape more than an in-position c-bet does, because the caller's positional advantage can otherwise chew you up on subsequent streets.

sections.title: Scenario: Exploiting Loose Callers
lines: Chapter ten, section three. Scenario, exploiting loose callers.
In the previous scenario we assumed the caller defended at equilibrium; now consider a real opponent who defends too widely.
A loose caller keeps too many hands in her range, especially the ones with weak equity or awkward playability.
Out of position, you can exploit this by c-betting more often, but with a shift toward smaller sizes that let her call with the marginal hands you dominate.
The value bet has a wider net: hands like queen-jack that would be too thin against a tight caller are now clearly ahead, and you can bet them for two streets confidently.

The bluff has a wider net too: hands like ace-high with backdoor equity that would have been vulnerable against a good defender now show good expected value against a loose caller's overcalling range.
The main danger is that against a loose caller, you will get to the turn and river more often, and being out of position means you need a real plan for both.
Turn barrels should be picked with river follow-through in mind, and semi-bluffs should have equity to fall back on when the caller does not fold.
The exploit is not to overbet every flop; it is to widen your c-bet range at the correct sizes so that the loose caller's mistakes on every street compound in your favor.
Out-of-position exploitation demands discipline, because you will pay for spew more often here than in position.

sections.title: Test Yourself
lines: Chapter ten, section four. Test yourself.
Question one. You three-bet from the small blind and the big blind calls. Flop is king-eight-two rainbow. Should you c-bet often or slow down?
C-bet often. This flop hits your range hard: ace-king, king-queen, and premium pairs are all disproportionately in your range compared to the big blind's.
Question two. Same start, flop is nine-eight-seven with two hearts. Adjust.
C-bet less often and more polarized. The board hits the big blind's calling range better; your c-bet range should shrink to top value plus best semi-bluffs, with lots of checking.
Question three. You c-bet out of position and get raised on a dynamic board. What is your default response with a medium hand?
Fold most medium hands. Out of position, defending against raises is expensive, and only your best value and highest-equity draws are worth continuing.
Question four. You are out of position with a strong range but a loose caller behind you. Should you c-bet larger or smaller than equilibrium?
Smaller. Loose callers reward wide c-bet ranges at small sizes, because the marginal hands you dominate keep calling and the marginal bluffs you fire keep getting through.
Practicing out-of-position c-betting is about knowing when your range advantage is enough to force through the disadvantage of being first to act.

sections.title: Conclusion
lines: Chapter ten, section five. Conclusion.
Out-of-position c-betting is the harder half of the aggressor's world, because you lose information on every street.
The framework is still the same as in-position play, but the shapes shift: c-bet less often, more polarized, and bigger, and defend a wider checked range instead of stabbing marginal spots.
Against equilibrium callers, out-of-position c-betting is best used sparingly and precisely, with a plan for both being raised and being called.
Against loose callers, the c-bet range widens and the sizes shrink, because their mistakes multiply against a well-tuned attack.

The one habit to internalize is that being out of position is a real cost, and every c-bet should either earn back that cost through a genuine range advantage or leverage a specific opponent tendency.
In the final chapter we shift to tournament play, where antes, ICM, and shrinking stacks add a whole new layer to every decision we have studied so far.

sections.title: Overview & Objectives
lines: Chapter eleven, section one. Overview and objectives.
Everything we have studied so far was implicitly assuming cash-game economics, where a dollar is a dollar no matter how many chips you have.
In tournaments, the value of a chip depends on your stack, on the payout structure, and on how many players are left, and that changes the math of almost every decision.
This chapter is about the two biggest tournament adjustments: playing with antes and adjusting for the independent chip model, or ICM.
By the end of this chapter you should be able to explain why antes make every pot bigger relative to the stacks, and why that pushes optimal strategies toward wider ranges and shorter fights.
You should be able to apply ICM adjustments to shove and call decisions on the money bubble and at the final table, where chip preservation is worth more than raw chip accumulation.
You should be able to reason about final-table clairvoyance games, where survival value makes even nut-versus-nothing situations trickier than a cash game would suggest.

And you should understand the general principle that tournament play amplifies the value of pot control and dampens the value of thin-edge aggression when you have a large stack and the ICM incentives point toward survival.

sections.title: Scenario: Playing With Antes
lines: Chapter eleven, section two. Scenario, playing with antes.
Antes are small mandatory contributions from every player before the hand starts.
The effect is that the pre-flop pot is much bigger relative to the blinds, and the pot odds on every pre-flop call improve for everyone.
The first consequence is that opening ranges widen, especially from late position, because the increased dead money in the pot makes marginal opens directly profitable.
The second consequence is that defenders in the blinds should defend wider than they would without antes, because they are getting a much better price.
The third consequence is that steal attempts, three-bet bluffs, and squeezes all become more profitable, because the increased dead money changes the fold-equity math.
The fourth consequence is that stack-to-pot ratios shrink faster, so a hand that would be a fine multi-street plan in a no-ante game becomes a stack-off spot with antes in play.
The overall effect is that ante games are more aggressive and more compressed, and stack management matters more than it does in the ante-free version of the same game.

As you sit down to a tournament with antes, expect to open wider from late position, defend wider from the blinds, and re-open wider when facing pre-flop action; those are the baseline adjustments the ante economics demand.

sections.title: The Independent Chip Model (ICM)
lines: Chapter eleven, section three. The independent chip model, or ICM.
ICM is a way of translating your chip stack into an expected share of the prize pool, based on the payout structure and the stacks of everyone still in the tournament.
The key insight is that chips you win are worth less than chips you lose, in ICM terms, because the payout structure is heavily weighted toward the top places.

That asymmetry means every decision you make near the money bubble or the final table should be biased toward chip preservation, and it changes the profitability of aggressive plays that would be clear winners in a chip-EV world.
For example, calling an all-in with slight positive chip equity may be a losing decision in ICM terms if your call risks a huge stack drop that would demolish your tournament equity.

The mirror is that shoving on other players who are ICM-pressured is doubly profitable: your fold equity is higher because they cannot afford to call marginally, and every fold gives you dead antes and blinds.
ICM is a heavy calculation to do at the table, but a few rules of thumb carry most of the value.
Rule one: the closer you are to a pay jump, the tighter you should call all-ins and the wider you should shove into short stacks.
Rule two: the bigger your stack advantage over the medium stacks, the more aggressively you should pressure them, because their ICM incentive is to fold.
Rule three: when you are the medium stack, avoid marginal spots with the big stacks and prey on the short stacks who cannot risk a call.

sections.title: Scenario: Clairvoyance at the Final Table
lines: Chapter eleven, section four. Scenario, clairvoyance at the final table.
Return one more time to the clairvoyance game, but now imagine the two players are at a tournament final table with three players remaining and a big ICM cliff between second and third place.
Ivan has an ace or a queen, Opal has a king, and Ivan can bet or check as in the original game.
In the cash-game version, we solved this game with a specific bluffing frequency for the queen and a specific calling frequency for the king.
At the final table, the ICM cost of losing the pot is much larger than the ICM gain of winning it, especially for the shorter stack.

The correct adjustment is that Opal's calling frequency should shrink, because the ICM cost of a wrong call is amplified, and Ivan's bluffing frequency with the queen should shrink in response, because he now needs less bluffing to make Opal indifferent.
Notice the direction of the adjustment: less action from both sides, more folding, and less thin value pursuit.
That is the general final-table ICM lesson: the game gets more conservative for both players when the payoff of a loss is much worse than the payoff of a win.
The polarized attacker keeps most of the leverage, but he has to spend it more carefully, and the bluff-catcher has to accept a lower expected value from her showdown holdings.
When you feel a hand tightening up on you at the final table, that instinct is often ICM speaking, and following it is usually the right call.

sections.title: Test Yourself
lines: Chapter eleven, section six. Test yourself.
Question one. You are the button in a tournament with antes and everyone folds to you. Should you open wider than you would without antes?
Yes. The dead money from antes gives you better pre-flop odds, and more marginal opens become directly profitable.
Question two. You are the medium stack at a final table with a huge pay jump between fourth and third. A short stack shoves under the gun. What is your calling range?
Tight. You should call only with hands that dominate his shoving range, because a call that busts you costs a huge ICM chunk.
Question three. You are the big stack at the same final table. The medium stack opens for a modest raise. What is your default response?
Aggressive. Three-bet often, because the medium stack cannot afford to call or four-bet you marginally, and every fold gives you dead money without ICM risk.
Question four. On the money bubble, you have an unimportant stack size. Should you open wider or tighter than you would deeper in the tournament?

Wider than deeper, but the correct answer depends on the immediate opponents; against ICM-pressured stacks, widen further, and against equally desperate stacks, tighten up because the fold equity vanishes.
Understanding ICM is the difference between a good cash player and a good tournament player.

sections.title: Conclusion
lines: Chapter eleven, section seven. Conclusion.
Tournament play is a version of the same game we have studied, but with a currency that fluctuates: chips are worth more or less depending on your stack, the payouts, and the number of players left.
Antes make every pre-flop pot bigger relative to the stacks and push optimal strategy toward wider ranges and shorter fights.
ICM changes the profitability of aggression: it pressures short and medium stacks to fold and lets big stacks bully them for dead chips.
The final-table clairvoyance scenario showed that even a purely polarized game gets tighter under ICM, because the loss cost outweighs the win gain.
The habit to keep from this chapter is asking, before every all-in decision, whose ICM pressure is heaviest right now and how that changes the incentives at the table.
The book closes with a short conclusion that ties the eleven chapters together and sends you off with the shape of the argument in one clean piece.

sections.title: Putting It All Together
lines: Conclusion, section one. Putting it all together.
The eleven chapters you just walked through are really one long argument about how to think about poker before the river.
The argument starts with leverage: on early streets, betting is not just about the current pot, it is about the leverage those bets carry into future streets.
Polarized ranges benefit from leverage, condensed ranges are punished by it, and every early-street decision is really a decision about which side of that asymmetry you want to be on.

The middle chapters gave you the mechanics: protection and semi-bluffing for hands that live between value and air, range construction as the discipline of choosing which hands do which job, and using leverage on real boards with real hand distributions.

The later chapters challenged the assumptions: what happens when the stacks are short, when the pre-flop caller has the range advantage, when the aggressor is out of position, or when tournament economics reshape the value of every chip.
In every case, the answer was some structured adjustment to the same core toolkit, not a wholesale reinvention.
Carry that structured way of thinking into every hand you play, and you will find that even unfamiliar spots start to feel navigable.

sections.title: The Habits That Matter Most
lines: Conclusion, section two. The habits that matter most.
If you leave this book with only five habits, make it these.
One: before every early-street decision, ask which shape your range wants to be, polarized, condensed, or linear.
Two: before every barrel, sort the incoming turn or river card into good, bad, or neutral for your range.
Three: pick your bet size to grow the pot geometrically toward the future bet you actually want to make.
Four: build your ranges from pure strategies first and use mixed strategies to balance them, so that the load-bearing hands drive the plan.
Five: check SPR and ICM context before you commit chips, because the value of every future action depends on them.
None of these habits is glamorous, and none of them wins a specific hand.
But apply them together, over thousands of hands, and you will find yourself in the right shape at the right time much more often than the players you are competing with.
Range construction is a lifetime skill, not a chapter to be finished, and the toolkit you built here is meant to keep sharpening as you use it.

sections.title: Where to Go From Here
lines: Conclusion, section three. Where to go from here.
The natural next step is to bring these ideas to the tools you already use: a solver, a training site, or a heads-up display in your online play.
When you run scenarios in a solver, look for the pure-strategy hands first, then the shape of the mixed strategies, and finally the exact frequencies.
When you review a session, focus on the range shapes you constructed rather than the individual results; a bad river outcome does not mean the range plan was wrong.
When you play, keep the good-turn, bad-turn, neutral-turn triage in the front of your mind, and let it govern your barreling frequency.

And when you find yourself in an unfamiliar spot, remember that the whole book is about the shape of ranges and the shape of leverage; almost any surprise decision can be interrogated by asking what those shapes want to look like here.
Poker is a game where the deepest players never quite finish learning, and that is the good news: every session is an opportunity to sharpen the same set of habits a little further.
Thank you for listening, and may your ranges be well constructed.
